mind.blurb: LSD, psychic spies and a cat wired for sound.

flags.name: False Flags
flags.blurb: Staged attacks, fake witnesses, a corpse with secret plans.

sky.name: The Sky Files
sky.blurb: Flying discs, Area 51 and signals from deep space.

bureau.name: The Bureau
bureau.blurb: Wiretaps, poison-pen letters and the JFK verdict.

bodies.blurb: When the government experimented on its own people.

hoax.blurb: The famous theories that fall apart when you dig.

cold.blurb: A nuke in space, a plan to bomb the Moon, a carrier made of ice.

watch.blurb: Telegrams, tech giants and a church that bugged the IRS.

unsolved.blurb: Vanished hijackers, ghost ships and a book nobody can read.

cases.hook: The CIA secretly dosed Americans with *LSD* to learn mind control.
ev: Approved in [[1953]] by CIA director [[Allen Dulles]].
Run by chemist [[Sidney Gottlieb]] for about [[20 years]].
In 1973 the director ordered the files [[destroyed]].
cases.truth: Project MKUltra ran from 1953 to 1973. The CIA gave LSD and other drugs to people, some of whom never knew, while searching for interrogation and mind-control methods. Most records were destroyed in 1973, but about 20,000 pages survived because they had been misfiled. They surfaced through a FOIA request and were aired at a 1977 Senate hearing.
src: US Senate hearing on Project MKUltra, 1977
cases.reveal: The CIA ran it for twenty years. Most files were destroyed, but twenty thousand pages survived and were read out in the Senate in 1977.
cases.title: Project MKUltra
cases.tease: the CIA spent twenty years trying to control the human mind

cases.hook: The CIA ran *safehouse brothels* to drug clients and watch what happened.
ev: Narcotics agent [[George White]] ran the San Francisco flat.
Men were slipped [[LSD]] without knowing.
Agents watched through [[one-way mirrors]].
cases.truth: Operation Midnight Climax was an MKUltra subproject. From the mid-1950s into the 1960s, sex workers paid by the CIA brought men to safehouses in San Francisco and New York, where they were drugged while agents observed. It came to light in the 1977 Senate hearings.
cases.reveal: It was an MKUltra subproject. Paid sex workers lured men to CIA flats in San Francisco and New York, where agents watched them get drugged.
cases.title: Operation Midnight Climax
cases.tease: the CIA rented flats, hired women, and watched through the mirrors

cases.hook: The US military paid *psychics* to spy on the Soviet Union.
ev: Code names included [[Grill Flame]] and [[Star Gate]].
Viewers tried to see [[distant targets]] with their minds.
It ran for nearly [[two decades]].
cases.truth: From the 1970s to 1995 the Army, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the CIA funded "remote viewing" units. A 1995 review commissioned by the CIA found it had never produced intelligence anyone could act on, and the program was closed. The CIA posted thousands of pages online in 2017.
cases.reveal: The Army, the DIA and the CIA funded psychic spies until 1995. A review found they never produced intelligence anyone could use.
cases.title: the Stargate psychic spies
cases.tease: the Pentagon paid people to spy on the Soviets with their minds

cases.hook: The CIA tried to turn a *cat* into a walking microphone.
ev: A microphone was implanted in the [[ear canal]].
The antenna ran along the [[tail]].
The project was dropped in [[1967]].
cases.truth: Acoustic Kitty was a real 1960s CIA project. A heavily redacted memo released in 2001, "Views on Trained Cats", says it worked technically but was impractical. The famous story that the cat was run over by a taxi on its first mission comes from a former official and is disputed.
src: CIA memo "Views on Trained Cats", released 2001
cases.reveal: The CIA really did wire up a cat. A 2001 memo called the idea workable but impractical. The taxi story is disputed.
cases.title: Acoustic Kitty
cases.tease: the CIA tried to send a cat on a spy mission

cases.hook: America's top generals signed a plan to stage *fake terror attacks* to start a war.
ev: Signed by Joint Chiefs chairman [[Lyman Lemnitzer]].
Ideas included a fake [[hijacking]] and blowing up a ship at [[Guantanamo]].
Every attack would be blamed on [[Cuba]].
cases.truth: Operation Northwoods was a March 1962 proposal from the Joint Chiefs of Staff to create pretexts for invading Cuba. The Kennedy administration rejected it. The document was declassified in 1997 by the Assassination Records Review Board.
cases.reveal: The Joint Chiefs signed it in March 1962. Kennedy's team rejected it, and the plan stayed secret until 1997.
cases.title: Operation Northwoods
cases.tease: America's top generals signed off on fake terror attacks

cases.hook: The August 4 attack that pushed the US deeper into *Vietnam* never happened.
ev: The ships were the [[USS Maddox]] and [[USS Turner Joy]].
Congress passed the Tonkin resolution [[three days]] later.
An [[NSA]] historian later found the intercepts were mishandled.
cases.truth: An August 2 clash was real, but the reported second attack on August 4, 1964 almost certainly did not happen. The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution followed on August 7. A study by NSA historian Robert Hanyok, declassified in 2005, concluded the signals intelligence had been misread and misrepresented.
src: NSA history by Robert Hanyok, declassified 2005
cases.reveal: The August 2 clash was real. The August 4 attack almost certainly never happened, and an NSA history admitted the intercepts were misread.
cases.title: the Gulf of Tonkin
cases.tease: a war escalated over an attack that never happened

cases.hook: The tearful teenage witness who helped sell the *Gulf War* was the ambassador's daughter.
ev: She said soldiers took babies from [[incubators]].
PR firm [[Hill & Knowlton]] helped prepare the testimony.
Her father was Kuwait's [[ambassador to the US]].
cases.truth: In October 1990 a 15-year-old known only as Nayirah testified to a congressional caucus about atrocities in a Kuwaiti hospital. In 1992 it emerged she was the daughter of Kuwait's ambassador and that the hearing was tied to a PR campaign for Citizens for a Free Kuwait. Later investigations found no support for her account.
cases.reveal: Nayirah was the Kuwaiti ambassador's daughter, and her testimony was tied to a PR campaign. Investigators found no support for her story.
cases.title: the Nayirah testimony
cases.tease: a crying teenager sold a war, and nobody checked who she was

cases.hook: British spies fooled Hitler with a *dead man* carrying fake invasion plans.
ev: The body was dressed as "Major [[William Martin]]".
It washed ashore in [[Spain]].
The real target was [[Sicily]].
cases.truth: Operation Mincemeat put forged letters on the body of Glyndwr Michael and floated it off the Spanish coast. German intelligence believed the papers and moved forces toward Greece and Sardinia before the Allies invaded Sicily in July 1943.
cases.reveal: The body of Glyndwr Michael carried forged letters. Hitler's spies believed them, and the Allies landed in Sicily in July 1943.
cases.title: Operation Mincemeat
cases.tease: a dead man fooled Hitler

cases.hook: The US Army fought part of WWII with *inflatable tanks*.
ev: The unit was the [[23rd Headquarters Special Troops]].
It used rubber tanks, fake radio traffic and [[recorded sound]].
Its work stayed secret for about [[50 years]].
cases.truth: The "Ghost Army" was about 1,100 artists, sound engineers and radio operators who staged fake units to mislead German forces in Europe. Its records stayed classified until the 1990s.
cases.reveal: Eleven hundred artists and sound engineers faked whole divisions with rubber tanks and speakers. It stayed secret for fifty years.
cases.title: the Ghost Army
cases.tease: an army of artists fought with rubber tanks

cases.hook: The US Army announced it had captured a *flying disc*.
ev: The press release came from [[Roswell Army Air Field]].
The next day it became a [[weather balloon]].
In 1994 the Air Force named it [[Project Mogul]].
cases.truth: On July 8, 1947 the base really did announce a "flying disc". The story was changed to a weather balloon the next day. In 1994 the Air Force said the debris came from Project Mogul, a classified balloon program built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. There was a cover-up. It just wasn't about aliens.
cases.reveal: The base really announced a flying disc. In 1994 the Air Force said it was Project Mogul, a secret balloon built to spy on Soviet nukes.
cases.title: Roswell
cases.tease: the US Army told the papers it had captured a flying disc

cases.hook: The CIA officially admitted *Area 51* exists.
ev: It was built to test the [[U-2]] spy plane.
The admission came through a [[FOIA]] request.
Spy planes explain many [[UFO reports]] of the era.
cases.truth: In 2013 a declassified CIA history of the U-2, obtained by the National Security Archive, named Area 51 and showed it on a map. A CIA study published in 1997 said high-flying reconnaissance planes accounted for many UFO reports in the late 1950s and 1960s.
cases.reveal: A declassified CIA history named Area 51 in 2013. It was built to test spy planes, and those planes explain a lot of UFO sightings.
cases.title: Area 51
cases.tease: the base the government wouldn't admit existed

cases.hook: The US Air Force logged *701 UFOs* it could never explain.
ev: The study was called [[Project Blue Book]].
It collected [[12,618]] sighting reports.
It was shut down in [[1969]].
cases.truth: Project Blue Book ran from 1952 to 1969. Of 12,618 reports, 701 stayed "unidentified". The Air Force said none showed a threat to national security or technology beyond known science. The records are held at the US National Archives.
src: US National Archives, Project Blue Book
cases.reveal: Project Blue Book logged 12,618 reports from 1952 to 1969. 701 were never identified.
cases.title: Project Blue Book
cases.tease: the Air Force logged 701 UFOs it could never explain

cases.hook: Navy pilots chased a *Tic Tac-shaped* object that outflew their jets.
ev: It happened near the carrier [[USS Nimitz]].
The lead pilot was Commander [[David Fravor]].
The Pentagon officially released the video in [[2020]].
cases.truth: In November 2004 Navy aviators off southern California reported a white, wingless object with no visible propulsion. The Defense Department formally released the infrared video in April 2020. The object remains officially unidentified.
cases.reveal: The Pentagon released the video in 2020. The object has never been officially identified.
cases.title: the Tic Tac UFO
cases.tease: Navy pilots chased something that outflew their jets

cases.hook: A radio telescope caught a *72-second signal* from space that nobody can explain.
ev: Detected by the [[Big Ear]] telescope in Ohio.
An astronomer circled it and wrote "[[Wow!]]".
It has never been [[detected again]].
cases.truth: The Wow! signal, recorded on August 15, 1977, was strong, narrow and close to the hydrogen line, exactly the kind of signal SETI looks for. It never repeated. Natural explanations have been proposed, including hydrogen clouds, but none is settled.
cases.reveal: The Wow! signal was strong, narrow and near the hydrogen line. It never repeated, and no explanation is settled.
cases.title: the Wow! signal
cases.tease: 72 seconds of signal from deep space, never heard again

cases.hook: The FBI mailed Martin Luther King Jr. an *anonymous letter* urging him to kill himself.
ev: The program was called [[COINTELPRO]].
It was exposed by a [[break-in]] at an FBI office in 1971.
The burglars stayed anonymous for [[43 years]].
cases.truth: COINTELPRO ran from 1956 to 1971 and targeted civil rights, antiwar and other groups. In 1964 the FBI sent King a letter and tape widely read as urging suicide. The program was exposed after activists took files from an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, in March 1971, and the Church Committee later confirmed it.
cases.reveal: The FBI ran COINTELPRO from 1956 to 1971. Activists exposed it by stealing files from an FBI office, and the Senate confirmed it.
cases.title: COINTELPRO
cases.tease: the FBI mailed a letter to Martin Luther King Jr.

cases.hook: The CIA had hundreds of *American journalists* secretly helping it.
ev: A 1977 report counted about [[400]] journalists.
The reporter was [[Carl Bernstein]].
The name "Mockingbird" belonged to a [[1963 wiretap]].
cases.truth: The Church Committee confirmed the CIA had relationships with journalists and news organizations, and Carl Bernstein reported in 1977 that about 400 American journalists had secretly assisted the agency. Whether "Operation Mockingbird" was one big media-control program is disputed: in the CIA's own "Family Jewels" files, Project Mockingbird is a 1963 wiretap of two reporters.
cases.reveal: The Church Committee confirmed CIA ties to journalists. Whether one big program called Mockingbird existed is still disputed.
cases.title: Operation Mockingbird
cases.tease: the CIA had friends in America's newsrooms

cases.hook: A US government committee concluded JFK was *probably killed in a conspiracy*.
ev: It was the [[House Select Committee on Assassinations]].
Its key evidence was a police [[audio recording]].
In 1982 scientists said the audio [[didn't hold up]].
cases.truth: In 1979 the committee concluded Kennedy was "probably assassinated as a result of a conspiracy", mostly because of an acoustic analysis of a police dictabelt recording. A National Academy of Sciences panel rejected that analysis in 1982. The National Archives has since released most remaining JFK records, including a large batch in 2025.
cases.reveal: The House committee said probably a conspiracy in 1979. Scientists later rejected the audio evidence it relied on.
cases.title: the JFK verdict
cases.tease: a government committee said JFK was probably killed in a conspiracy

cases.hook: US health officials let hundreds of Black men go *untreated for syphilis* for 40 years.
ev: The study ran from [[1932 to 1972]].
[[Penicillin]] was the standard cure by the late 1940s.
It ended after an [[AP reporter]] broke the story.
cases.truth: The US Public Health Service study enrolled about 600 Black men in Alabama, 399 of whom had syphilis, and withheld treatment to watch the disease progress. Jean Heller of the Associated Press exposed it in 1972. President Clinton formally apologized in 1997.
src: CDC, The Syphilis Study at Tuskegee
cases.reveal: The Public Health Service withheld treatment from Black men in Alabama for forty years. President Clinton apologised in 1997.
cases.title: the Tuskegee study
cases.tease: health officials watched men go untreated for forty years

cases.hook: The US Navy secretly sprayed *bacteria* over San Francisco.
ev: The test was called Operation [[Sea-Spray]].
A ship released the bacteria [[off the coast]].
Nobody in the city was [[told]].
cases.truth: In September 1950 the Navy released Serratia marcescens and Bacillus bacteria to see how a biological attack would spread over a city. Soon after, a cluster of rare Serratia infections appeared at a San Francisco hospital and one patient died, though a link was never proven. The test became public in the 1970s.
cases.reveal: In 1950 the Navy sprayed bacteria over San Francisco to test a germ attack. Nobody in the city was told.
cases.title: Operation Sea-Spray
cases.tease: the Navy sprayed bacteria over San Francisco

cases.hook: After WWII the US quietly hired *Nazi scientists* and cleaned up their records.
ev: The program was Operation [[Paperclip]].
More than [[1,600]] German scientists and engineers came over.
The best known was rocket engineer [[Wernher von Braun]].
cases.truth: Operation Paperclip brought German scientists, many of them former Nazi Party members, to work for the US. Some background files were rewritten to get them past immigration rules. Von Braun went on to lead development of the Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo to the Moon.
cases.reveal: More than 1,600 German scientists came to the US. Some files were cleaned up, and Wernher von Braun went on to build the Moon rocket.
cases.title: Operation Paperclip
cases.tease: America quietly hired Nazi scientists

cases.hook: The Moon landings were *filmed in a studio*.
ev: Astronauts brought back [[382 kg]] of Moon rock.
Mirrors left on the Moon are still hit by [[lasers]] today.
A NASA orbiter [[photographed]] the landing sites from 2009.
cases.truth: Six Apollo missions landed between 1969 and 1972. The samples, the laser reflectors and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photos of the descent stages and footpaths all point the same way. The Soviet Union tracked the missions and never disputed them.
cases.reveal: Moon rock, laser mirrors still in use and orbiter photos of the landing sites all say the same thing. They went.
cases.title: the Moon landing hoax
cases.tease: they say the Moon landings were filmed in a studio

cases.hook: In 1943 the Navy made a warship *invisible* and teleported it.
ev: The ship was the destroyer escort [[USS Eldridge]].
The story began with letters from "[[Carlos Allende]]".
The Navy says its records [[don't match]].
cases.truth: The "Philadelphia Experiment" traces back to letters written in the 1950s by Carl Allen, who used the name Carlos Miguel Allende. The Navy says no such experiment took place, and the ship's records don't fit the story.
src: US Naval History and Heritage Command
cases.reveal: The story began with letters from a man called Carl Allen. The Navy says it never happened.
cases.title: the Philadelphia Experiment
cases.tease: a warship supposedly vanished into thin air

cases.hook: Ships and planes vanish in the *Bermuda Triangle* more than anywhere else.
ev: Insurer [[Lloyd's of London]] doesn't treat it as extra risky.
The US Coast Guard [[doesn't recognize]] it as a danger zone.
It's one of the [[busiest]] stretches of ocean on Earth.
cases.truth: Studies have found no more disappearances there than in other heavily travelled waters. Many famous cases were exaggerated, misdated or happened somewhere else. Storms and the Gulf Stream explain the real losses. The name itself was coined by a magazine writer in 1964.
cases.reveal: The Triangle has no more disappearances than any other busy stretch of ocean. The legend came from a 1964 magazine story.
cases.title: the Bermuda Triangle
cases.tease: a patch of ocean that supposedly swallows ships

cases.hook: Paul McCartney *died in 1966* and was replaced by a lookalike.
ev: Fans hunted for [[clues]] on album covers.
The rumor peaked in [[1969]].
Life magazine's cover: "[[Paul is still with us]]".
cases.truth: The "Paul is dead" rumor spread through US college papers and radio in 1969, fed by fans reading clues into album art and backwards lyrics. McCartney gave Life magazine an interview that November to deny it. He's still touring.
cases.reveal: The rumour spread in 1969. Paul McCartney told Life magazine he was alive and well. He is still touring.
cases.title: Paul is dead
cases.tease: fans swore a Beatle died in 1966

cases.hook: *Birds aren't real.* They're government surveillance drones.
ev: The movement began in [[2017]].
Its founder is [[Peter McIndoe]].
In 2021 he confirmed it was [[satire]].
cases.truth: Birds Aren't Real is a parody conspiracy theory made to mock misinformation. Its "believers" hold rallies and put up billboards. McIndoe said publicly in 2021 that it had been a joke from the start.
cases.reveal: Birds Aren't Real is a joke. Its founder confirmed in 2021 that it was satire from the start.
cases.title: Birds Aren't Real
cases.tease: a movement claims every bird is a government drone

cases.hook: US diplomats were hit by a secret *energy weapon* in Havana.
ev: Symptoms were first reported in [[2016]].
In 2023 most US spy agencies called a foreign attack [[very unlikely]].
Many of those affected still [[disagree]].
cases.truth: Hundreds of US personnel reported headaches, dizziness and strange sounds. A 2023 intelligence assessment found a foreign adversary very unlikely to be responsible, and 2024 NIH studies found no evidence of brain injury. Some officials and many of those affected dispute those findings, so the case stays open.
src: Office of the Director of National Intelligence, 2023
cases.reveal: A 2023 assessment found a foreign attack very unlikely, but many of those affected disagree. The case is still open.
cases.title: Havana syndrome
cases.tease: diplomats said they were hit by an invisible weapon

cases.hook: The US set off a *nuclear bomb in space* and lit up the sky over Hawaii.
ev: It exploded [[400 km]] above the Pacific.
Its yield was about [[1.4 megatons]].
The pulse knocked out about [[300 streetlights]] in Hawaii.
cases.truth: Starfish Prime was a high-altitude nuclear test on July 9, 1962. The blast created artificial auroras seen across the Pacific, and its electromagnetic pulse damaged electrics in Hawaii, about 900 miles away.
cases.reveal: Starfish Prime exploded 400 kilometres up in July 1962. It made artificial auroras and knocked out streetlights in Hawaii, 900 miles away.
cases.title: Starfish Prime
cases.tease: America set off a nuclear bomb in space

cases.hook: The US Air Force drew up a plan to *nuke the Moon*.
ev: The plan was called Project [[A119]].
A young [[Carl Sagan]] worked on it.
It stayed secret until [[2000]].
cases.truth: Project A119 was a 1958 Air Force study of detonating a nuclear bomb on the Moon, partly as a show of strength. It was never carried out. A former NASA executive, Leonard Reiffel, revealed it in 2000.
cases.reveal: Project A119 was a real 1958 study. It never went ahead, and a former NASA executive revealed it in 2000.
cases.title: Project A119
cases.tease: the Air Force had a plan to nuke the Moon

cases.hook: The US Army planned to hide *nuclear missiles under the Greenland ice*.
ev: The plan was called Project [[Iceworm]].
Its public cover was a research base called [[Camp Century]].
Denmark never gave [[consent]].
cases.truth: Project Iceworm aimed to build a network of mobile nuclear missile sites under the Greenland ice sheet. Camp Century was publicized as a scientific base. The missiles were never installed, and Denmark was not asked.
cases.reveal: Camp Century was the cover story. The real plan was a missile network under the ice. It was never built, and Denmark was never asked.
cases.title: Project Iceworm
cases.tease: the Army hid a missile plan under the Greenland ice

cases.hook: The CIA used Howard Hughes as cover to *steal a sunken Soviet submarine*.
ev: The ship was the [[Hughes Glomar Explorer]].
The cover story was [[seabed mining]].
The target was the Soviet sub [[K-129]].
cases.truth: Project Azorian raised part of the Soviet submarine K-129 from the Pacific floor in 1974. The CIA paid for a giant ship, presented as Howard Hughes's deep-sea mining venture.
cases.reveal: Project Azorian was real. The CIA built a giant ship, called it a Howard Hughes mining project, and lifted part of a Soviet sub in 1974.
cases.title: Project Azorian
cases.tease: the CIA used a billionaire as cover to steal a Soviet submarine

cases.hook: Britain tried to build an *aircraft carrier out of ice*.
ev: The material was ice mixed with [[wood pulp]].
It was nicknamed [[pykrete]].
A prototype was built on a lake in [[Canada]].
cases.truth: Project Habakkuk was a Second World War plan for a giant ship made of pykrete to hunt U-boats in the mid-Atlantic. A prototype floated on Patricia Lake in Alberta before rising costs killed it.
cases.reveal: Project Habakkuk got as far as a prototype on a Canadian lake. Then costs rose, and longer-range planes made it pointless.
cases.title: Project Habakkuk
cases.tease: Britain tried to build an aircraft carrier out of ice

cases.hook: The FBI trained ordinary Alaskans as *secret spies* for a Soviet invasion.
ev: The program was Operation [[Washtub]].
Recruits were [[fishermen, pilots and trappers]].
It ran until Alaska became a [[state]].
cases.truth: Operation Washtub was a 1950s Air Force and FBI plan to plant stay-behind agents across Alaska in case the Soviet Union invaded. It ran from 1951 to 1959.
cases.reveal: Operation Washtub ran from 1951 to 1959. The idea was a ready-made spy network if the Soviets ever occupied Alaska.
src: Declassified FBI and Air Force records
cases.title: Operation Washtub
cases.tease: the FBI trained Alaskan fishermen as secret spies

cases.hook: NATO countries kept *secret armies* hidden across Europe for decades.
ev: Italy's branch was called [[Gladio]].
The prime minister admitted it to parliament in [[1990]].
They were built to fight a [[Soviet invasion]].
cases.truth: Operation Gladio was Italy's part of a network of clandestine stay-behind forces set up across Western Europe after the Second World War. Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti revealed it in October 1990.
cases.reveal: Italy's prime minister revealed Gladio in 1990. Similar stay-behind networks existed across Western Europe.
cases.title: Operation Gladio
cases.tease: secret armies were hidden across Europe for forty years

cases.hook: The US military tried to *weaponize the weather* in Vietnam.
ev: Planes seeded clouds over the [[Ho Chi Minh Trail]].
The goal was a longer [[monsoon]].
Its slogan was "make [[mud]], not war".
cases.truth: Operation Popeye ran from 1967 to 1972, seeding clouds to extend the rainy season and turn enemy supply routes to mud. It led to a 1977 treaty banning environmental warfare.
cases.reveal: Operation Popeye seeded clouds from 1967 to 1972. The outcry led to a treaty banning weather warfare.
cases.title: Operation Popeye
cases.tease: the US military tried to weaponise the weather

cases.hook: For 30 years, the NSA read copies of *Americans' international telegrams*.
ev: The program was called [[SHAMROCK]].
Telegraph companies handed over copies [[every day]].
At its peak the NSA analysed [[150,000]] messages a month.
cases.truth: Project SHAMROCK began in 1945 and ran until it was exposed by Congress in 1975. Western Union and other companies gave the agency copies of international telegrams.
cases.reveal: Project SHAMROCK ran from 1945 until Congress exposed it in 1975. Telegraph companies quietly handed over the messages.
cases.title: Project SHAMROCK
cases.tease: for thirty years, the NSA read Americans' telegrams

cases.hook: The NSA ran a secret program to collect data from *Google, Facebook and Apple*.
ev: The program was called [[PRISM]].
It was leaked by contractor [[Edward Snowden]].
The story broke in [[June 2013]].
cases.truth: PRISM collected internet communications from US tech companies under a surveillance law. Snowden's leaks were published by The Guardian and The Washington Post on June 6, 2013. The companies denied giving direct access to their servers.
cases.reveal: PRISM was revealed in June 2013 from Edward Snowden's leaks. The companies said the government never had direct access to their servers.
cases.title: PRISM
cases.tease: the NSA had a program to pull data from Google, Facebook and Apple

cases.hook: The CIA secretly spied on *American anti-war protesters*.
ev: The program was Operation [[CHAOS]].
It kept files on [[7,200]] Americans.
A [[New York Times]] reporter exposed it in 1974.
cases.truth: Operation CHAOS ran from 1967 to 1974, looking for foreign links to the anti-war movement. It never found the foreign control it was searching for. Seymour Hersh exposed it in The New York Times.
cases.reveal: Operation CHAOS ran from 1967 to 1974 and kept files on 7,200 Americans. Seymour Hersh exposed it.
cases.title: Operation CHAOS
cases.tease: the CIA spied on American anti-war protesters

cases.hook: The Church of Scientology *infiltrated the US government* and stole its files.
ev: It was called Operation [[Snow White]].
The main target was the [[IRS]].
In 1977 the [[FBI]] raided church offices.
cases.truth: Operation Snow White was one of the largest infiltrations of the US government in history. Eleven church executives, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted of crimes including burglary of government offices.
cases.reveal: Operation Snow White was real. After a 1977 FBI raid, eleven church executives were convicted, including Mary Sue Hubbard.
src: United States v. Mary Sue Hubbard, 1979
cases.title: Operation Snow White
cases.tease: a church infiltrated the US government

cases.hook: Lightbulb makers secretly agreed to make bulbs *burn out faster*.
ev: The group was called the [[Phoebus cartel]].
They capped bulb life at [[1,000 hours]].
Makers were [[fined]] for bulbs that lasted longer.
cases.truth: The Phoebus cartel, formed in 1924 by companies including Osram, Philips and General Electric, standardized bulb life at 1,000 hours, down from about 2,500, and fined members whose bulbs lasted too long.
cases.reveal: The Phoebus cartel formed in 1924. Members were fined if their bulbs lasted more than a thousand hours.
cases.title: the Phoebus cartel
cases.tease: lightbulb makers agreed to make bulbs die sooner

cases.hook: Factory workers were told glow-in-the-dark *radium paint was safe* to put in their mouths.
ev: They painted [[watch dials]].
They shaped their brushes with their [[lips]].
Many died of [[radiation poisoning]].
cases.truth: The Radium Girls were told the paint was harmless and were taught to point their brushes on their lips. Many fell gravely ill. Their lawsuits helped establish workers' rights to sue over occupational disease.
cases.reveal: The Radium Girls were told the paint was harmless. Many died, and their lawsuits changed worker safety law.
cases.title: the Radium Girls
cases.tease: factory workers were told glowing paint was safe to lick

cases.hook: Volkswagen built cars that *knew when they were being tested*.
ev: Hidden software was called a [[defeat device]].
It was in about [[11 million]] cars.
Volkswagen pleaded [[guilty]] in 2017.
cases.truth: Volkswagen diesels ran cleanly only during emissions tests. The US EPA exposed it in September 2015, and the company later pleaded guilty to criminal charges.
cases.reveal: Dieselgate broke in 2015. About eleven million cars had the cheat software, and Volkswagen pleaded guilty.
cases.title: Dieselgate
cases.tease: cars that knew when they were being tested

cases.hook: The sugar industry *paid Harvard scientists* to point the finger at fat.
ev: The scientists were paid about [[$6,500]].
The payments were [[never disclosed]].
Historians uncovered it in [[2016]].
cases.truth: In the 1960s a sugar industry group paid three Harvard scientists for a review that played down sugar's role in heart disease. Researchers revealed the documents in 2016.
cases.reveal: A sugar industry group paid for the 1960s review. The documents came out in 2016.
cases.title: the sugar papers
cases.tease: the sugar industry paid Harvard scientists to blame fat

cases.hook: A hijacker jumped out of a jet with *$200,000* and was never found.
ev: He called himself [[Dan Cooper]].
He jumped somewhere over the [[Pacific Northwest]].
In 1980 a boy found [[$6,000]] of the cash by a river.
cases.truth: On November 24, 1971, a man hijacked a Boeing 727, collected a ransom and parachuted into the night. The FBI suspended its active investigation in 2016. He has never been identified.
cases.reveal: D. B. Cooper was never identified. The FBI suspended its active investigation in 2016.
cases.title: D. B. Cooper
cases.tease: a hijacker jumped out of a jet with two hundred thousand dollars and vanished

cases.hook: Amateur codebreakers cracked the Zodiac killer's cipher *51 years* later.
ev: The cipher had [[340]] characters.
It was mailed to a newspaper in [[1969]].
It was solved by a team of [[private citizens]].
cases.truth: The Z340 cipher was decoded in December 2020 by David Oranchak, Sam Blake and Jarl Van Eycke. The killer himself has never been identified.
cases.reveal: The 340 cipher was solved in December 2020 by three amateurs. The killer has never been identified.
cases.title: the Zodiac cipher
cases.tease: amateurs cracked a killer's code fifty-one years later

cases.hook: A ship was found sailing with *no one on board*, and its crew was never seen again.
ev: She was found off the [[Azores]].
The cargo of [[alcohol]] was still there.
The [[lifeboat]] was missing.
cases.truth: The Mary Celeste was found adrift and deserted on December 4, 1872, seaworthy and with belongings untouched. What made the crew abandon ship has never been established.
cases.reveal: The crew of the Mary Celeste was never found. Nobody knows why they left a seaworthy ship.
cases.title: the Mary Celeste
cases.tease: a ship found sailing with nobody on board

cases.hook: A 600-year-old book is written in a *language nobody can read*.
ev: It's called the [[Voynich manuscript]].
Its pages were carbon-dated to [[1404 to 1438]].
It's kept at [[Yale]].
cases.truth: The Voynich manuscript is full of strange plants, stars and bathing figures, written in a script that has never been deciphered, despite efforts by wartime codebreakers.
cases.reveal: The Voynich manuscript has never been deciphered. Nobody knows if it's a code, a language or a hoax.
cases.title: the Voynich manuscript
cases.tease: a six-hundred-year-old book nobody can read

cases.hook: Nine hikers fled their tent into a frozen night and died. *Nobody knew why*.
ev: It happened in the [[Ural Mountains]].
Their tent was cut open [[from the inside]].
A 2021 study pointed to an [[avalanche]].
cases.truth: Nine Soviet hikers died at Dyatlov Pass in February 1959. Russian investigators concluded in 2020 that an avalanche most likely drove them out, and a 2021 study showed how a slab avalanche could explain the injuries.
cases.reveal: For sixty years it was a mystery. Now investigators think a small slab avalanche drove them out into the cold.
cases.title: the Dyatlov Pass
cases.tease: nine hikers cut their way out of their own tent and ran into the snow

cases.hook: US airmen reported a *UFO landing* in an English forest.
ev: It happened near the base at [[RAF Woodbridge]].
The deputy commander, [[Charles Halt]], wrote a memo.
Sceptics blame a [[lighthouse]].
cases.truth: In December 1980 US Air Force personnel reported strange lights in Rendlesham Forest, Suffolk. Sceptics explain it as a fireball, the Orfordness Lighthouse and bright stars.
cases.reveal: The memo is real. Sceptics point to a lighthouse and a fireball. Believers still call it Britain's Roswell.
cases.title: Rendlesham Forest
cases.tease: US airmen reported a UFO landing in an English forest

cases.hook: A dead man on a beach carried a hidden note that said *"It is finished"*.
ev: He was found near [[Adelaide]], Australia.
The note read "[[Tamám shud]]".
A 2022 DNA study [[named]] him.
cases.truth: The Somerton Man was found dead on December 1, 1948. In 2022 researchers used genetic genealogy to say he was Carl Webb, an engineer, though how he died is still unknown.
cases.reveal: In 2022 researchers said DNA showed he was Carl Webb. How he died, and what the note meant, is still unknown.
cases.title: the Somerton Man
cases.tease: a dead man on a beach carried a note that said it is finished

cases.hook: The famous 1934 photo of the *Loch Ness Monster* is real.
ev: It was called the [[surgeon's photograph]].
The head was sculpted onto a [[toy submarine]].
The hoax was confessed in [[1994]].
cases.truth: The surgeon's photograph was a hoax. The monster was a model fixed to a toy submarine, built by Christian Spurling.
cases.reveal: The surgeon's photograph was a model on a toy submarine. The hoax came out in 1994.
cases.title: the Loch Ness photo
cases.tease: the most famous monster photo ever taken

cases.hook: Crop circles are made by *something that isn't human*.
ev: Two men, [[Doug Bower and Dave Chorley]], came forward.
They said they started in [[1978]].
They used [[planks and rope]].
cases.truth: In 1991 Bower and Chorley took credit for more than 200 crop circles in England and showed reporters how they did it. Crop circles then spread worldwide.
cases.reveal: In 1991 two men in England showed how they made more than two hundred crop circles with planks and rope.
cases.title: crop circles
cases.tease: perfect circles appearing overnight in English fields

cases.hook: The ship that sank wasn't the Titanic. It was her *sister ship, swapped* for insurance.
ev: The sister ship was the [[Olympic]].
Each ship had its own yard number, Titanic's was [[401]].
Parts stamped [[401]] were found on the wreck.
cases.truth: The switch theory comes from a 1998 book. Titanic's yard number, 401, has turned up on parts recovered from the wreck, while Olympic's fittings carry 400.
cases.reveal: Parts recovered from the wreck carry Titanic's own yard number, 401. The ship that sank was the Titanic.
cases.title: the Titanic switch
cases.tease: some say the ship that sank wasn't the Titanic

cases.hook: A secret antenna field in Alaska *controls the weather*.
ev: The site is called [[HAARP]].
It studies the [[ionosphere]], high above the weather.
It's run by the [[University of Alaska]].
cases.truth: HAARP is an ionosphere research facility. The ionosphere sits far above where weather forms. The University of Alaska Fairbanks has run it since 2015 and holds public open days.
cases.reveal: HAARP studies the ionosphere, far above where weather happens. A university runs it and opens it to the public.
cases.title: HAARP
cases.tease: an antenna field in Alaska that supposedly controls the weather

cases.hook: The Great Wall of China is *visible from the Moon*.
ev: The Moon is about [[384,000 km]] away.
From there, the Wall is like a [[hair]] seen from 3 km.
The myth dates back to [[1754]].
cases.truth: The Great Wall is far too narrow to see with the naked eye from the Moon. The idea appears in a letter written in 1754, long before anyone went to space.
cases.reveal: From the Moon, the Wall is like a human hair seen from three kilometres away. The myth is older than spaceflight.
cases.title: the Great Wall myth
cases.tease: a wall you can supposedly see from the Moon

cases.hook: Plane trails are *chemicals sprayed on purpose*.
ev: Scientists surveyed in 2016: [[77]].
Who found evidence of a secret program: [[1]].
Contrails are mostly [[ice crystals]].
cases.truth: A 2016 survey of 77 atmospheric scientists found 76 had seen no evidence of a secret spraying program. Contrails form when hot, humid exhaust freezes in cold air.
cases.reveal: In a 2016 survey, 76 out of 77 atmospheric scientists had seen no evidence. Contrails are frozen water vapour.
cases.title: chemtrails
cases.tease: the trails behind planes, and what people think is in them

cases.hook: Thousands saw a giant *UFO over Phoenix*.
ev: It happened on [[March 13]], 1997.
Planes from Operation [[Snowbird]] were in the area.
The lights were [[A-10 jets]] and flares.
cases.truth: The Phoenix Lights were real lights, but both sightings have been explained: a formation of A-10 jets, and later illumination flares dropped on a training range.
cases.reveal: The lights were real, but they were A-10 jets and flares from a training exercise.
cases.title: the Phoenix Lights
cases.tease: thousands of people saw lights over Phoenix

cases.hook: A former intelligence officer told Congress the US has *non-human craft*.
ev: His name is [[David Grusch]].
He testified on [[July 26]], 2023.
The Pentagon's UFO office found [[no evidence]].
cases.truth: Grusch testified under oath about a crash-retrieval program he said he was told about. No evidence has been presented, and the Pentagon's AARO says it found nothing to back the claims.
cases.reveal: The testimony was real and under oath. The evidence never appeared, and the Pentagon says it found none.
cases.title: the UFO hearing
cases.tease: a former intelligence officer told Congress about non-human craft

cases.hook: The CIA admitted it helped *overthrow Iran's elected government*.
ev: The prime minister was [[Mohammad Mosaddegh]].
Britain's [[MI6]] was in on it.
The US released the files in [[2013]].
cases.truth: The 1953 coup removed Mosaddegh after he nationalized Iran's oil industry. In August 2013, on the coup's 60th anniversary, the US released documents showing it was involved.
cases.reveal: The coup happened in 1953 after Iran nationalised its oil. The US released the documents in 2013.
cases.title: Operation Ajax
cases.tease: the CIA helped topple an elected government, then admitted it

cases.hook: The CIA plotted to kill Fidel Castro with a *poisoned diving suit*.
ev: The Church Committee counted [[eight]] plots.
One idea was a suit laced with [[tuberculosis]].
Castro died of [[old age]] in 2016.
cases.truth: The 1975 Church Committee documented at least eight CIA plots to kill Castro between 1960 and 1965, including the contaminated diving suit.
cases.reveal: The Senate found at least eight CIA plots. Castro outlived them all.
cases.title: the Castro plots
cases.tease: the CIA tried to kill Castro with a poisoned diving suit

cases.hook: US officials secretly *sold weapons to Iran* to fund rebels in Nicaragua.
ev: The rebels were the [[Contras]].
Congress had [[banned]] funding them.
The president was [[Ronald Reagan]].
cases.truth: The Iran-Contra affair centered on secret arms sales to Iran. Proceeds were diverted to the Contras despite laws that barred further funding.
cases.reveal: Iran-Contra was real. Arms money went to the Contras in defiance of Congress.
cases.title: Iran-Contra
cases.tease: weapons for Iran, money for rebels, and Congress kept in the dark

cases.hook: Government scientists collected *dead babies' bodies* to measure nuclear fallout.
ev: The study was Project [[Sunshine]].
About [[1,500]] bodies were sampled.
Parents often [[weren't told]].
cases.truth: Project Sunshine measured strontium-90 from nuclear tests in human remains. Many of the samples came from babies and young children, often without their parents' knowledge.
cases.reveal: Project Sunshine took samples from about fifteen hundred bodies, many of them babies, often without telling the parents.
cases.title: Project Sunshine
cases.tease: scientists collected bodies to measure fallout

cases.hook: Hospital patients were secretly *injected with plutonium*.
ev: The first was [[Ebb Cade]], in 1945.
It happened at [[Oak Ridge]], Tennessee.
Patients [[weren't told]].
cases.truth: During and after the Manhattan Project, some hospital patients were injected with plutonium without their knowledge, to study how it moved through the body.
cases.reveal: The plutonium injections were real. Patients weren't told, and the US government later investigated the experiments.
src: Advisory Committee on Human Radiation Experiments, 1995
cases.title: the plutonium files
cases.tease: hospital patients were secretly injected with plutonium

cases.hook: A giant *ape-man* is hiding in the forests of North America.
ev: The famous film was shot at [[Bluff Creek]], California.
It lasts just under [[60 seconds]].
In 2002 a family revealed [[carved wooden feet]].
cases.truth: Bigfoot sightings rest on folklore, misidentified animals and hoaxes, and scientists don't recognise it as a real animal. The Patterson–Gimlin film from October 1967 is still debated, but no body, bones or DNA have ever been found. After Ray Wallace died in 2002, his family revealed the carved wooden feet he had used to make giant footprints since 1958.
cases.reveal: No bones, no body, no DNA. And in 2002 one man's family revealed the wooden feet he used to fake the footprints.
src: Bigfoot research and the Wallace family, 2002
cases.title: Bigfoot
cases.tease: a giant ape-man supposedly walks the forests of North America

cases.hook: The Earth is *flat* and the government is hiding it.
ev: A Greek scholar measured Earth's [[circumference]] around 240 BC.
He did it with [[shadows]] in two cities.
Ships vanish over the horizon [[hull first]].
cases.truth: Eratosthenes worked out the size of the round Earth more than 2,000 years ago by comparing shadow angles in two Egyptian cities. Ships sinking hull-first over the horizon, the curved shadow on the Moon during an eclipse, and photos from space all show the same thing.
cases.reveal: A Greek scholar measured the round Earth with shadows over two thousand years ago. Ships, eclipses and space photos all agree.
cases.title: Flat Earth
cases.tease: millions of people say the Earth is flat

cases.hook: The *Illuminati* was a real secret society.
ev: It was founded on [[1 May 1776]] in Bavaria.
Its founder was a law professor, [[Adam Weishaupt]].
Bavaria [[banned]] secret societies in the 1780s.
cases.truth: The Bavarian Illuminati was an Enlightenment society that wanted to curb the power of the church and the nobility. It had a few hundred verifiable members before the Bavarian government banned secret societies in the 1780s and it collapsed. The modern idea that it secretly runs the world has no evidence behind it.
cases.reveal: It was real, and it was crushed in the 1780s. The idea that it still secretly runs the world has no evidence at all.
cases.title: the Illuminati
cases.tease: the secret society that really existed

cases.hook: Elvis *faked his death* in 1977 and went into hiding.
ev: He died on [[16 August 1977]] at Graceland.
Fans point to the spelling [[Aaron]] on his grave.
A famous 1987 sighting was at a [[Burger King]].
cases.truth: Elvis Presley died at Graceland on 16 August 1977. Theorists say the spelling Aaron on his gravestone is a clue, but he used both Aron and Aaron during his life. The 1987 sighting at a Burger King in Kalamazoo turned sightings into a running joke.
cases.reveal: He died at Graceland in 1977. The gravestone spelling is no clue: he used both spellings while he was alive.
cases.title: Elvis is alive
cases.tease: fans swear the King of Rock and Roll faked his own death
